body:
You are drafting spoken lines for a video game. Reply with plain text only, in the exact row format given at the end of this message. Do not send messages to anyone else and do not ask questions: decide. Write nothing but the rows (no title, no notes, no Markdown).

THE GAME. "The Crooked Moon" is a single-player, turn-based tactical party RPG built from a folk-horror Dungeons and Dragons campaign. It is set in Wickermoor Hollow, a haunted valley in Druskenvald, a land of endless night under a giant Crooked Moon with a crone's face. The look is a Halloween that never ends, drawn like an 1980s cartoon. A ghost train, the Ghostlight Express, has crashed in the valley; the party is stranded in the Hollow and its village, Wickermoor. The tone is warm, wry and funny on the surface, with real dread and real grief underneath. The player controls a party of four chosen from six companions: Rook Coldwake, Tobin Hayward, Silas Vane, Delphine Ravelle, Lucan Houndstooth and Cordelia Skein. They are quirky, capable adults.

THE NARRATOR. A NARRATOR row is spoken by the Vagrant, the green-skinned ferryman of the ghost train, who tells the tale in a folksy Southern drawl. At the camp fire he is warm and wry, and when a talk turns sad his humour leaves and he goes plain and level. He speaks to the party as "you" and about the companion in the third person, by first name. Present tense, one or two sentences, under about 32 words. Concrete senses (a smell, a sound, a touch, what the hands are doing) over adjectives. Never tell the player what to feel. Never "suddenly". No facts the party could not see. Drop the final g ("hangin'") in about one Narrator row in four, and use no other dialect spelling. He is kind, never mocks a stumble and never makes light of the dead.

RULES FOR EVERY LINE.
1. The companion's voice sheet below comes first. Match its accent, pace, vocabulary and contractions, and the existing lines. Use a pet phrase at most twice in the whole reply and never twice in one talk. Never repeat or closely paraphrase a line already in the voice sheet or the note.
2. A SAY row is the companion speaking: one or two short sentences, under about 28 words. Never put three sentences in one row; start another row instead.
3. The party's options (OPTION rows) are under 12 words, in the plain voice of the party, work at any hour and in any weather, never name a hero, and are never rolls or checks. A reply must always answer the option it follows.
4. Canon limits. Use only the facts in the voice sheet and the note below. Do not invent a new named person, place, monster, event, object the companion carries, or piece of the companion's history. You may invent small, harmless habits, fondnesses, superstitions and turns of phrase, and the look of the fire and the night. Name no place that the note does not name. Never state a dark secret. You may come close to one and step back.
5. Nothing here is a game system: no dice, no checks, no points, no levels, no HP, no "approval", no menus talked about aloud. Plain punctuation only (commas, full stops, hyphens, apostrophes, question marks, quotation marks inside a line when someone is quoted). No em dashes, no semicolons, no brackets, no asterisks, no stage directions, no placeholders.
6. Humour comes from the character, never explained. The sad turn is plain and short.
7. Our own words. Nothing quoted from any book.

THIS REQUEST. Region banter for Wickermoor Village: 8 short exchanges between two or three companions, spoken as the party walks about this place. There are no Narrator rows, no options and no replies. Every row is a companion talking to another companion, never to the player.

HOW IT WORKS. When the party comes into an area, now and then one exchange plays as a few lines of chat between companions who happen to be in the party, once each. Only two or three of the six are ever in the party, so each exchange stands alone, mentions nobody else and needs no setup. Each one below is about what is in front of the party in one place at one moment of the story. Banter is funny first; one line in an exchange may turn honest, never more. The chat is about the place: what it looks and smells like, what is odd or sad or silly in it, and how each companion's trade, habits and fears meet it.

RULES.
1. Each exchange is 4 to 6 SAY rows, each a companion's single line (one or two short sentences, under about 28 words), alternating naturally between the speakers; every speaker listed speaks at least once.
2. Use only the facts in the attached cast sheets and the "In front of them" facts of that exchange. The "Story now" line is everything the party knows of the story: a remark must never run ahead of it (name a villain, a fight or a result only if the Story now line does). Never state or hint at any companion's past or secret, and never say what anyone's debt is. No new named people, places or monsters.
3. Pet words and phrases: each companion's at most once in an exchange, and never in two consecutive lines. Companions call each other by first name.
4. No two exchanges may share a joke or a topic, and no line may repeat a line in a cast sheet. Spread the topics: do not make every exchange about the same kind of thing.
5. Plain punctuation only (commas, full stops, hyphens, apostrophes, question marks, quotation marks). No em dashes, semicolons, brackets, asterisks or stage directions. No game terms. Our own words.
AVOID in this region: The Connection scenes (Mori Shade, Sister Rain, Holly Aster, Alda Farnum, Hilda Brom, Thomasin Ardor and what they say to a companion) belong to the companions: do not stage them. Name villagers only as the place facts do. The Crooked House's inside, the Rookery's boss and Fool's Day's villain are not to be described.

THE EXCHANGES (in this order):
EXCHANGE 1: Silas + Delphine + Lucan (speaker ids: silas_vane, delphine_ravelle, lucan_houndstooth)
  Story now: The party is new to the village. The Crooked House on the hill above is still haunted and the storm has not ended. Lucan's hound is only ever called Dreadfang.
  Talk about: the Oak of Many Faces and the Founder's statue, and the odd feel of a village under a storm.
  In front of them: Wickermoor Village: The hub: a village round a trodden square, an oak of carved faces, a clocktower, the Silverbell along the south and the crooked estate on its hill. Timber-framed houses with steep roofs crowd round a trodden square where a faceless statue stands on one side and a gnarled oak, bark carved all over with faces, on the other. A clocktower rises over the village and the river runs... Parts of it: The Founder's Round; The north row; The moor road; The estate's hill; The west quarter; The south-west lanes; The east side; The south side. Things to see: The Founder's statue; The oak's roots; The clocktower; The pavilion; The Green Queen's sign; The well; A bone bonfire, banked; A wicker hare; A carved turnip over a door. People here: Old Rusty; Sister Rain; Jeremiah Stover; Gaston Doray; Hilda Brom.
EXCHANGE 2: Rook + Tobin + Cordelia (speaker ids: rook_coldwake, tobin_hayward, cordelia_skein)
  Story now: The party is at the inn. The Crooked House on the hill above is still haunted.
  In front of them: The Green Queen Inn: The Green Queen Inn, a room of Wickermoor Village. The inside of The Green Queen Inn: candle-lit, close and creaking. Parts of it: The Green Queen Inn. Things to see: The bar; The taproom hearth; The little stage; The kitchen counters; A board of rumours. People here: Alda Farnum; Bess Crumley.
EXCHANGE 3: Silas + Cordelia (speaker ids: silas_vane, cordelia_skein)
  Story now: The Crooked House has been cleansed and the storm is over. The party is back in the village, with Act Two still ahead.
  Talk about: how the village looks and sounds now the storm has ended: the clocktower, the square, the people about.
  In front of them: Wickermoor Village: The hub: a village round a trodden square, an oak of carved faces, a clocktower, the Silverbell along the south and the crooked estate on its hill. Timber-framed houses with steep roofs crowd round a trodden square where a faceless statue stands on one side and a gnarled oak, bark carved all over with faces, on the other. A clocktower rises over the village and the river runs... Parts of it: The Founder's Round; The north row; The moor road; The estate's hill; The west quarter; The south-west lanes; The east side; The south side. Things to see: The Founder's statue; The oak's roots; The clocktower; The pavilion; The Green Queen's sign; The well; A bone bonfire, banked; A wicker hare; A carved turnip over a door. People here: Adela Druskenvald; Hilda Brom; Sister Rain; Weston Murdoch; Old Rusty.
EXCHANGE 4: Rook + Silas (speaker ids: rook_coldwake, silas_vane)
  Story now: Two of the five Act Two places are behind the party; the village goes about its business.
  In front of them: Bread by Holly: Bread by Holly, a room of Wickermoor Village. The inside of Bread by Holly: candle-lit, close and creaking. Parts of it: Bread by Holly. Things to see: The bread oven; Cooling racks; Sacks of flour. People here: Holly Aster; Violet; Lavender.
EXCHANGE 5: Rook + Delphine (speaker ids: rook_coldwake, delphine_ravelle)
  Story now: All five Act Two places are behind the party. Act Three has begun and the end is near.
  Talk about: how small and precious the village feels with the end near: the notice board, the oak, the Green Queen's sign.
  In front of them: Wickermoor Village: The hub: a village round a trodden square, an oak of carved faces, a clocktower, the Silverbell along the south and the crooked estate on its hill. Timber-framed houses with steep roofs crowd round a trodden square where a faceless statue stands on one side and a gnarled oak, bark carved all over with faces, on the other. A clocktower rises over the village and the river runs... Parts of it: The Founder's Round; The north row; The moor road; The estate's hill; The west quarter; The south-west lanes; The east side; The south side. Things to see: The Founder's statue; The oak's roots; The clocktower; The pavilion; The Green Queen's sign; The well; A bone bonfire, banked; A wicker hare; A carved turnip over a door. People here: Sister Rain; Old Rusty; Jeremiah Stover; Gaston Doray; Hilda Brom.
EXCHANGE 6: Rook + Lucan (speaker ids: rook_coldwake, lucan_houndstooth)
  Story now: The Roving Rookery has come to the valley: a dovecote that walks. Its keeper, a hag called Golub Graygullet, has not been dealt with. Lucan's hound may be called Barnaby now and is known to fear thunder.
  In front of them: The Dovecote: the Parcel Store: The ground floor of the walking dovecote: crates and letters and a constant cooing. The inside of a round dovecote: straw, seed, feathers, crates piled in drifts of letters, and a ladder going up to the roost. Parts of it: The parcel store. Things to see: Albert's nest of stolen ribbon; Sacks of seed; Drifts of undelivered letters; Coils of leather cord; A round window, with the moor moving past.
EXCHANGE 7: Tobin + Delphine (speaker ids: tobin_hayward, delphine_ravelle)
  Story now: It is the Festival of Fools. The village has swollen to three times its size, hung with ribbon, and there is no way out. Chuckles has not been dealt with.
  In front of them: The Festival of Fools: Wickermoor Village swollen to three times its size, strung with ribbon and ringing with carnival music, with no way out that stays out. The village is the wrong size. The streets twist back on themselves between buildings stuffed to the rafters with hand pies, ribbons run roof to roof in green, red and gold, and in the middle of a square that used to be round a ma... Parts of it: The Absurd Streets; Festival Square; The Prize Counter; A shuttered door. Things to see: A clown balloon the size of a cart; Ribbons, roof to roof; A bonfire; The crowd, closing in; The crowd of dancers; Dancers shoving to the music; A building packed to the rafters with scotch eggs and hand pies; A costumed dancer, not stopping; The road out, west. People here: The Beekeeper; The Bell Sewer; The Blinkered Rider; The Stilted Drummer; The Horned Bear.
EXCHANGE 8: Rook + Tobin (speaker ids: rook_coldwake, tobin_hayward)
  Story now: The party has found the Silent Church, the one place the festival cannot reach. Chuckles has not been dealt with.
  In front of them: The Silent Church: The half-rebuilt Brightsinger chapel, the one place the festival cannot reach. The carnival music stops at the door as if cut with a knife. Tarps hang where the windows will go, new timber smells of resin, and a knight in marble twice a man's height stands before the altar with a sneer on his stone face. Parts of it: The Silent Church. Things to see: The altar, half rebuilt; The stone knight watches the door; Tarps where the windows will go; New timber, still sweet with resin.

THE ROW FORMAT (exact). One row per line:

EXCHANGE <number>
SAY <speaker id>: <line>
SAY <speaker id>: <line>
...

Use the speaker ids exactly as given (for example SAY rook_coldwake: ...). Write exactly 8 EXCHANGE blocks, numbered 1 to 8, and nothing else.

ATTACHED DOCUMENTS. Two documents come attached to this message; read both before you write: `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/banter-cast-1.md` (the voice sheets and fact lists for Rook Coldwake, Tobin Hayward and Silas Vane) and `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/banter-cast-2.md` (the same for Delphine Ravelle, Lucan Houndstooth and Cordelia Skein).
result:
EXCHANGE 1
SAY silas_vane: Look at the mugs carved into that oak, Delphine, every one of 'em pulling a worse poker face than the faceless gent across the mud.
SAY delphine_ravelle: At least the Founder's statue knows how to hold a pose, darling, though billing yourself without a nose is a bold choice for the square.
SAY lucan_houndstooth: The storm drives the damp right down from that crooked estate, if you please, and Dreadfang does not care for the spoor round the roots.
SAY silas_vane: Tell's in the twitch, friend, and when a whole village carves its worries into tree bark instead of skipping town, the house already owns the deed.
SAY delphine_ravelle: Then let them keep their soggy bark, Silas, because my hem is taking on water and I refuse to play to an empty square.

EXCHANGE 2
SAY tobin_hayward: Three paces back from the taproom hearth, Rook, the grease on those kitchen counters would take a spark quicker than dry clover.
SAY rook_coldwake: Chimney draw is sluggish, Tobin, and that board of rumours by the bar hasn't been cleared by a proper clerk in six months.
SAY cordelia_skein: Never mind the hearth, darling, the tallow smoke and warm ale are doing fascinating things to every pulse in this room.
SAY tobin_hayward: They are stewing in their own damp, Cordelia, and half the timber round that little stage has rot behind the wainscot.
SAY rook_coldwake: Settle down now, the roof holds the rain off, and a dry ledger by the bar is more than we had on the moor.

EXCHANGE 3
SAY silas_vane: Funny how quiet the square goes once the sky stops spitting, Cordelia, you can actually hear that clocktower ticking over the river.
SAY cordelia_skein: The barometric drop has eased, darling, and the villagers' heartbeats have slowed by a full third since the clouds broke over the hill.
SAY silas_vane: You call it pulse ratios, I call it folks stepping out by the well without checking if the roof's about to fold on 'em.
SAY cordelia_skein: It is a remarkably resilient little specimen of a town, Silas, even if Old Rusty by the pavilion smells entirely of wet iron.
SAY silas_vane: Give 'em an hour in the dry, friend, and somebody will be running a three-card shoe off the Founder's plinth.

EXCHANGE 4
SAY silas_vane: Best spot in the hollow, Rook, warm flour in the air and not a single thing on those cooling racks trying to bite my fingers off.
SAY rook_coldwake: Oven brickwork is sound and the sacks are stacked clear of the damp, though this warmth isn't doing my knuckles any favours, Silas.
SAY silas_vane: Right, forgot you frostbitten lads don't care for a snug bakehouse, I can shift my censer by the door if the heat's crowding you.
SAY rook_coldwake: Leave it be, lad, the yeast and lavender beats cellar mould, even if I can't recall the last time I ate a loaf.

EXCHANGE 5
SAY delphine_ravelle: Look at The Green Queen's sign swinging in the dark, Rook, it feels like the whole square could fit inside a hatbox tonight.
SAY rook_coldwake: Small parish, Delphine, doesn't take long to learn where the roots lift the cobbles by the oak or which roofs leak.
SAY delphine_ravelle: Your Foolishness hasn't made a single crack since we passed the well, and I think I might actually miss this muddy little stage when the curtain falls.
SAY rook_coldwake: Slabs are level and the folk know our names now, so we'll see the shift through properly before we pack the ledger.
SAY delphine_ravelle: Mind the seams, darling, you are going to make me sound sentimental in front of the turnip over that door.

EXCHANGE 6
SAY lucan_houndstooth: Good heavens, Rook, the moor is moving past that round window, and Barnaby is tucked so tight against my boots I can scarcely step.
SAY rook_coldwake: Complete violation of parish zoning, Lucan, a building has no business strolling across the turf with this many undelivered letters in storage.
SAY lucan_houndstooth: The cooing from the roost above is deafening, if you please, and some magpie has woven a whole nest of stolen ribbon beside the seed sacks.
SAY rook_coldwake: Unruly administration from cellar to rafters, and if that ladder isn't pegged to regulation, we'll be citing the keeper in person.
SAY lucan_houndstooth: Stay close by the leather cord, good boy, it is only floorboards groaning, not thunder.

EXCHANGE 7
SAY tobin_hayward: That building is packed to the rafters with hand pies and scotch eggs, Delphine, the crust is sweating right through the lath and plaster.
SAY delphine_ravelle: Never mind the pastry, Tobin, look at the cheap seats out here, ribbons strung roof to roof and a clown balloon the size of a cart.
SAY tobin_hayward: Keep between me and that bonfire in the square, the dancers are shoving too close and the whole street smells of hot suet.
SAY delphine_ravelle: Take my elbow, darling, I know how a rigged house works when the music won't stop, and we are not staying for the encore.
SAY tobin_hayward: Good soil, bad seed, and whatever stretched these lanes three times wide needs weeding at the taproot.

EXCHANGE 8
SAY tobin_hayward: Hear that, Rook, the horns and drums cut off right at the threshold like someone took shears to a briar.
SAY rook_coldwake: Good thick stone, Tobin, even with tarps over the windows, and the new timber round the altar is laid square.
SAY tobin_hayward: Sweet resin in the boards too, fresh pine, not a speck of festival rot or bonfire smoke on the air in here.
SAY rook_coldwake: Could do without the marble lad sneering at the door, mind, twice regulation height and blocking the main aisle.
SAY tobin_hayward: Let him sneer, so long as he keeps the sparks and the dancers on the other side of the step.
